title: Active Income Earns Deferral; Passive Income Comes Home Every Year
summary: When you own a company abroad, its profits are normally taxed at home only when they come home. Controlled-foreign-company rules make an exception for passive income, such as rent, interest and gains held in a foreign company you control, and tax it at home each year as if it had already arrived. Knowing which side of that line your income falls on decides whether deferral exists at all.
body:
A foreign company you control can usually hold its active business profits abroad without home tax until they come home, but passive income, such as rent, interest and investment gains, is often taxed at home every year whether or not a dollar moves.

Recall

Q. What are the three gates every distribution must pass?

A. The corporate-law test, such as solvency or distributable profit; the lender's distribution conditions; and withholding at the right rate, with the evidence that supports it.

Q. Can a tax treaty create a tax?

A. No. A treaty can only reduce or remove tax that domestic law already imposes.

Q. What is an estimate class?

A. A category describing how mature an estimate is, from early order-of-magnitude to definitive, with a wider expected accuracy range the earlier it is. It tells the reader how much to trust the number.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, last week we moved money home on purpose. This week asks a harder question: can your home country tax the money even if it never moves? For a company you control abroad, the answer is often yes, for the wrong kind of income. A developer who parks rental income in a low-tax foreign company, expecting to pay home tax only on distribution, may discover that home tax was due every year, with reporting forms he never filed. Deferral is valuable when it is real. This week teaches when it is.

Deferral, and why governments limit it

In plain English: a company is a separate taxpayer. If your foreign company earns profit and keeps it, you, the shareholder, have usually received nothing, so your home country has usually nothing to tax yet. That gap, between profit earned abroad and tax paid at home, is deferral.

The professional framing: deferral rewards real foreign business, which is legitimate. But it also invites a simple trick: move easily movable income, such as interest, rent, royalties and portfolio gains, into a company in a country with low or no tax, and leave it there indefinitely. Controlled-foreign-company rules, often shortened to CFC rules, exist to close that trick. In general terms, they say that if residents control a foreign company, and it earns passive income, that income is attributed to the resident shareholders and taxed at home each year, as though it had been paid to them [unverified — confirm independently]. Different countries call the rules by different names and draw the lines differently, so every element below must be verified against the primary source before you rely on it.

The three questions every CFC regime asks

Almost every regime asks three questions, in some form.

First, control. Is the foreign company controlled by home-country residents, alone or together, and sometimes counting related persons? Control is usually measured by votes or value, and many regimes have a minimum stake below which a shareholder is not caught at all.

Second, the character of the income. Is it active business income, earned by real people running a real business, or passive income, earned simply by owning assets? Interest, dividends from portfolio investments, royalties and many gains are usually passive. Rent is the tricky one: rental income is often treated as passive unless the company carries on an active rental business at a scale the rules define, for example with enough full-time staff managing the property [unverified — confirm independently].

Third, the tax already paid abroad. Many regimes give relief for foreign tax on attributed income, through a deduction or a credit, and some exempt companies taxed abroad at a rate close to the home rate, on the logic that there is little to gain from deferral there.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer resident in Country R owns 100 percent of a company in Country L, which taxes companies at a hypothetical 0 percent. The company owns a rented warehouse earning 500,000 dollars of net rent a year and employs no one; a local agent collects rent. Under a typical CFC regime, the company is controlled, the rent is passive, and no foreign tax was paid. The developer is taxed in R on 500,000 dollars a year as attributed income, whether or not the company pays a dividend. Deferral does not exist here. The low-tax company has added cost and reporting, and saved nothing.

Say that out loud now.

Control, character and foreign tax: those three questions decide whether deferral exists.

Active business: where deferral survives

A second worked example, hypothetical. The same developer instead owns a company in Country S, taxed at a hypothetical 25 percent, that develops and sells condominium units, employing a project team of twelve on site. Its profit of 2,000,000 dollars is active business income from a real development business. Under a typical regime, it is not attributed; home tax arises only when profit comes home as a dividend, and even then exemption or a credit may apply. Deferral is real, and it was earned by substance: people, decisions and risk, in S.

The line between the two examples is not the country or the asset; it is what the company does. A company that holds a building and collects rent through an agent is an investor. A company that develops, leases, manages and maintains property with its own staff can be a business. Where that line sits in your home country's rules is a question for a qualified adviser.

Reporting is a separate duty

Even where no tax is attributed, most countries require residents to report foreign affiliates, foreign property and foreign accounts each year, often on dedicated information returns, with penalties for late or missing filings that can apply even when no tax was owed [unverified — confirm independently]. Vera teaches that on Day 4. For today, hold one distinction: tax and reporting are two duties, and failing the second can cost money even when the first was clean.

How the best do it

Disciplined international owners classify every foreign entity once a year: controlled or not, active or passive, foreign tax rate, attribution expected, reports due, and who files them. The classification sits in the structure memo beside the chart, and any change of activity, such as a development company that finishes and becomes a rental holder, triggers a fresh review. A small developer can copy this with a single table.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: passive income in a controlled foreign company may be taxed at home yearly, removing deferral. Liability: missed information returns can carry penalties regardless of tax owed. Banking: lenders and banks ask about foreign affiliates in know-your-customer checks and expect consistent answers. Governance: activity in the foreign company must be real, run by its own people. Estate: attributed income and unfiled reports become your estate's problem if not cleaned up. Exit: a company that shifts from development to holding may shift from active to passive, changing the tax on what remains.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser in the home country on classification and attribution, and in the foreign country on local tax.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming a foreign company defers home tax because it pays no dividends, when its income is passive and attributed every year. The control is an annual classification of every foreign entity, signed off by a home-country adviser, before the tax year closes.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks low foreign tax is always good. For passive income in a controlled company, low foreign tax often means home tax at the full rate, every year, with no credit to soften it.

Callback

In Week 22, Elias taught residence versus source and flow-through entities. CFC rules are the residence country reaching through a company it would normally respect, for one kind of income, much as it already reaches through a flow-through entity for every kind.

Recap

Deferral means foreign profit is taxed at home only when it comes home. CFC rules remove deferral for passive income in controlled foreign companies, asking about control, the character of the income and foreign tax paid. Active business, built on real substance, usually keeps deferral. Reporting is a separate duty.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: a composite case of an offshore rental company that never filed.
checklist: I know which of my foreign companies are controlled by home-country residents.
I have classified each company's income as active or passive under home rules.
I know whether rental income counts as active business at its current scale.
I know the foreign tax rate each company pays and whether it affects attribution.
I know the information returns due for each foreign entity and who files them.
I review classification whenever a company's activity changes.
My structure memo records the classification for each entity, each year.
A home-country adviser signs off before the tax year closes.
head: Field checklist
speak: A foreign company is a separate taxpayer, so its profits are normally taxed at home only when they come home as a dividend. That gap is deferral. Controlled-foreign-company rules limit it. In general terms, if home residents control a foreign company and it earns passive income, such as interest, portfolio gains, royalties and often rent, that income is attributed to them and taxed at home every year, whether or not anything is paid out. Every regime asks three questions: control, the character of the income, and the foreign tax already paid. In my hypothetical, a zero-tax company holding a warehouse through an agent saved nothing: the rent was taxed at home each year. A development company with its own team, taxed abroad at a normal rate, kept its deferral. And separately from tax, most countries require yearly information returns on foreign affiliates, with penalties even when no tax is owed.
terms: Deferral — postponing home tax on foreign company profits until they are distributed to the shareholder.
Controlled-foreign-company rules — rules taxing home residents currently on certain income, usually passive, of foreign companies they control.
Passive income — income earned mainly from owning assets, such as interest, portfolio dividends, royalties and often rent, rather than from running an active business.

hostile.q: You hold the rental property through a low-tax foreign company. Why isn't all that rent taxed at home every year anyway?
hostile.a: It may be, and I have assumed it is unless we can show otherwise. Under our home country's rules, as our adviser reads them, rent is passive unless the company runs an active rental business at the scale the rules require. Ours does not yet, so I model the rent as attributed each year and taxed at home, with relief for any foreign tax. Any deferral is upside, not underwriting.

title: The Offshore Rental Company That Never Filed
summary: This is a composite example. A developer moved rental properties into a low-tax foreign company, assumed no home tax arose until dividends were paid, and never filed the home-country information returns on the company. Years later, attributed income, interest and reporting penalties arrived together, and a voluntary disclosure that might have limited them came too late.
body:
This is a composite example. A developer held rental property through a low-tax foreign company for six years, believing home tax would wait for a dividend, filed no information returns, and learned during a bank's due diligence that he owed six years of tax on income he had never received.

Recall

Q. How do you gross up a target net payment for withholding?

A. Divide the target by the share kept. To net 900,000 dollars after 10 percent withholding, pay 900,000 divided by 0.90, which is 1,000,000 dollars.

Q. What made the conduit company in Week 57 fail its treaty claim?

A. It had no real directors deciding, no control of its own bank account, and an obligation in practice to pass every dividend on within days, so it was not the beneficial owner.

Q. What does cost escalation mean in an estimate?

A. The expected rise in prices between the estimate date and when the work is bought or built, allowed for separately from contingency.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this failure is about tax and about records at once. Nothing in it was hidden from anyone on purpose. The developer simply believed a rule that is true for active business and false for passive income, and the reporting duty he did not know about turned a tax question into a penalty question. The point is not that offshore companies are wrong. It is that a structure's tax result depends on rules most people never read.

This is a composite example built from patterns that recur in cross-border holdings. The numbers are hypothetical round figures.

1. Timeline

Year 1: a developer resident in Country R transfers three rented townhouse buildings, through a sale at value, into a new company he owns 100 percent in Country L, which taxes companies at a hypothetical 0 percent. A local property agent collects rent and pays costs. Years 1 to 6: the company earns 400,000 dollars of net rent a year and pays no dividends, accumulating cash and buying a fourth building. Year 7: the developer applies to a home-country bank for a large construction loan. The bank's due diligence asks for his foreign affiliates' information returns. There are none. His new accountant reviews the structure and concludes that the rent was passive income attributed to him each year.

2. Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Choosing a zero-tax country for passive rental assets. Running the company through an agent with no staff of its own. And, every year, deciding not to ask a home-country adviser about it, because no money had come home and so, he assumed, there was nothing to report.

3. Assumptions

He assumed the foreign company was a wall: what happened inside it was not his income until it was paid out. That is true, in many systems, for active business. He assumed that if no tax was owed, no filing was needed. And he assumed that the transfer of the buildings into the company in year 1 had no home tax consequence, because it was "his own company". Each assumption was wrong in a different way, and the third is a reminder that moving property between your own entities can itself be a taxable disposition.

4. Incentives

The foreign service provider that formed the company was paid to incorporate and administer it, not to advise on home tax. The property agent was paid on rent collected. The developer's home accountant prepared his personal return from the documents he was given, and was never shown the foreign company. Nobody in the chain was engaged to look at the whole.

Say that out loud now.

No money came home is not the same as no tax and no filing.

5. Warning signs ignored

The service provider's engagement letter said in plain words that it gave no advice on the tax of any other country. The developer's personal tax return asked, in some form, whether he owned foreign property or companies, and the answer given was incomplete. A friend mentioned in year 3 that "those offshore rules" had caught someone they knew. And the company bought a fourth building with accumulated rent, a sign that passive income was building up exactly where the rules look.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the bank's question in year 7. Many countries offer a voluntary disclosure process in which a taxpayer who comes forward before an authority contacts them may get relief from some penalties, though usually not from the tax or interest [unverified — confirm independently]. Once a third party has identified the gap, and especially once an authority has, that relief may no longer be available, and the developer's choices narrowed to paying and explaining.

7. Root cause

The root cause was believing a foreign company defers home tax by being foreign, rather than by doing active business. The reporting failure followed from the same belief.

What it cost

The hypothetical arithmetic. Attributed rent of 400,000 dollars a year for six years is 2,400,000 dollars. At a hypothetical home rate of 30 percent, with no foreign tax to credit, home tax of 720,000 dollars. Add interest for each late year. Add penalties for six years of unfiled information returns, which in some systems are fixed amounts per return and in others a percentage of the value involved [unverified — confirm independently]. Add the possible home tax on the year-1 transfer of the buildings, if it was a taxable disposition at value. And the construction loan, the reason he was talking to the bank, was delayed by months while all of it was resolved. The company's cash, built up offshore, had to be repatriated to pay, through the doors Devika taught last week, with their own leakage.

What would have saved it

One meeting in year 1, with a home-country adviser shown the whole structure, before the buildings moved. The adviser would have asked the three CFC questions, flagged the transfer, and named the information returns. The developer might then have kept the buildings at home, or built a genuine active rental business abroad, or accepted yearly attribution knowingly and filed every year. All three are defensible. Guessing was not.

Cole adds an integrity note. Once the gap was found, the developer had two temptations: to describe the company to the bank as an active business it never was, or to file six years of returns quietly and hope no one compared dates. Either would have turned a compliance failure into a misrepresentation. The right course was the slow one: disclose to the bank what had been found, engage an adviser to correct the filings properly, and accept the cost.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a structure designed in one country by people who advise only on that country, with no one looking at the home side. The control is a home-country sign-off on every foreign entity before it is formed or funded, and every year after.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats information returns as paperwork that matters only when tax is owed. In many systems, the penalty for not filing applies whether or not any tax was due.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught engagement letters: what an adviser is, and is not, engaged to do. This case turns on one sentence in one: the service provider gave no advice on the tax of any other country. The developer read the sentence as boilerplate. It was the most important line in the file.

Recap

A developer moved rental property into a zero-tax foreign company, assumed home tax waited for a dividend, filed nothing, and found six years of attributed income, interest and penalties during a bank's diligence. Home-country sign-off on every foreign entity, before and every year, is the prevention.

Rule 59: Never form, fund or keep a foreign company without a home-country adviser classifying its income and naming its reports, in writing, before the first transfer and every year after; foreign is not the same as deferred.

Next: Warrick on The Money: what deferral is worth, and the contingent tax a foreign holding puts on your balance sheet.
checklist: A home-country adviser has reviewed every foreign entity I own.
I know whether each foreign company's income is attributed to me each year.
I have checked whether moving property into a company I own was a taxable disposition.
I file every information return on foreign affiliates and property, on time.
Each adviser's engagement letter states what they do not advise on, and I have filled the gap.
I know whether a voluntary disclosure process exists and when it stops being available.
I have modelled the cash needed to pay any attributed tax.
head: Field checklist
speak: This is a composite case. A developer moved three rented buildings into a company he owned in a zero-tax country, run by a local agent with no staff. He believed home tax would wait until the company paid him a dividend, so for six years he paid nothing and filed nothing at home. The rent was passive income in a company he controlled, so under his home country's controlled-foreign-company rules it was attributed to him every year. A bank's diligence for a new loan found no information returns. The result was six years of home tax on income he never received, interest, reporting penalties, possible tax on the original transfer, and a delayed loan, with voluntary disclosure relief likely gone because a third party found the gap first. The root cause was believing foreign means deferred. Rule 59: never form, fund or keep a foreign company without a home-country adviser classifying its income and naming its reports.
terms: Attributed income — income of a foreign company that the home country taxes in the hands of its resident shareholders as if received.
Information return — a filing that reports foreign property, accounts or affiliates to the tax authority, often required even when no tax is due.
Voluntary disclosure — a process in which a taxpayer corrects past non-compliance before being contacted, sometimes in exchange for reduced penalties.

hostile.q: Your personal statement shows a foreign company holding rental property. Where are its information returns for the last six years?
hostile.a: They are attached, each filed on time, with my home adviser's annual classification of the company's income. The rent is treated as attributed to me each year and is in my personal returns, with relief for foreign tax. If you want, my adviser will walk your credit team through the classification and the filings directly.

rule: Rule 59: Never form, fund or keep a foreign company without a home-country adviser classifying its income and naming its reports, in writing, before the first transfer and every year after; foreign is not the same as deferred.

title: What Deferral Is Worth, and the Tax You Owe Before You Are Paid
summary: Deferral is a loan from the government at zero interest, repaid when profit comes home. Its value is the present value of the tax postponed, and it grows with the length of the deferral and the gap between foreign and home rates. Attribution of passive income cancels it, and turns a foreign holding into a yearly cash call on its owner.
body:
Real deferral is an interest-free loan from your home government, repaid when the money comes home; attributed income is the opposite, a tax bill each year on cash you have not received, and your balance sheet has to carry both honestly.

Recall

Q. In a lender negotiation, what do you ask for when the lender wants your shareholder loan fully subordinated?

A. Accept priority, and ask that current interest be paid only when the distribution test is met, which is no more cash than the lender would allow as a dividend; you ask for the door, not for more cash.

Q. What three costs reduce a treaty rate's headline value?

A. The yearly cost of substance, the probability-weighted cost of denial, and any saving the home credit would have given anyway.

Q. How should contingency be structured in a project budget?

A. In layers with owners: design contingency, construction contingency and owner's contingency, each sized to the risks it covers and drawn down under rules.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a foreign company can make you richer by postponing tax, or poorer by taxing you on money you cannot spend. Which one depends on yesterday's three questions. Today we put numbers on both, and then put them where they belong: on your personal balance sheet, as an asset in one case and a liability in the other.

Deferral as an interest-free loan

In plain English: if home tax is due only when profit comes home, the tax you would have paid stays invested in the business until then, earning a return for you.

The professional framing: the value of deferral is the difference between paying home tax now and paying it later, discounted at your cost of capital. It grows with three things: the gap between foreign and home tax rates, the length of the deferral, and the return earned on the retained money.

A worked example, hypothetical, with rates chosen only for arithmetic. An active foreign development company earns 1,000,000 dollars, pays a hypothetical 15 percent foreign tax, and retains 850,000 dollars. Home tax on a dividend, after credit, would be a further 15 percent of the pre-tax profit, 150,000 dollars. If the company pays the dividend now, the owner pays 150,000 dollars now. If it reinvests for ten years and then pays, the 150,000 dollars is paid in year 10. At an 8 percent discount rate, the present value of 150,000 dollars in ten years is about 69,500 dollars. Deferral is worth about 80,500 dollars on this one year's profit, and that is before counting the return earned on the extra 150,000 dollars kept in the business.

Notice what deferral is not. It is not a permanent saving, unless the money never comes home, and money that never comes home is money you never spend. Deferral is a timing benefit with a value, not a rate cut.

Attribution reverses it

Now take a passive company in the same position. Its 1,000,000 dollars of profit is attributed to you yearly. With a hypothetical home rate of 30 percent and foreign tax of 15 percent credited, you owe 150,000 dollars at home this year, from your own pocket, because the company has not paid you anything. If the company's cash is committed, to a reinvestment or behind a loan covenant, you must find 150,000 dollars elsewhere.

Say that out loud now.

Deferral is a loan from the government; attribution is a tax bill on cash I have not received.

A second worked example. Over six years of attribution at 150,000 dollars a year, you pay 900,000 dollars of home tax while the company accumulates the cash. When the company eventually pays you a dividend from those attributed profits, many systems do not tax it again, because it was taxed already; the profit is often tracked in a special account for that purpose [unverified — confirm independently]. So the total tax may be the same as with an immediate dividend. What changes is your cash: you paid early, from personal funds, and the company holds the money. That is the worst combination for liquidity, and it is exactly the situation in the composite case on Day 2.

What the cash call does to a project

For a developer, the cash call has a second-order cost. The company holding passive income might also be the one funding a new project's equity, or securing a guarantee. Pulling cash out to pay the owner's attributed tax reduces what it can contribute, and lenders who see a sponsor paying personal tax from project cash will ask why. Plan the cash: either distribute enough each year to cover the attributed tax, which costs little if the dividend is not taxed again, or keep a personal reserve sized to it.

How the best do it

Sophisticated families with foreign holdings typically keep a tax provision schedule: for each entity, the tax deferred, the year it is expected to come due, the tax attributed and paid, and the cash set aside. It sits beside their personal balance sheet, so the true net worth is visible after the tax that is owed or will be. A small developer can copy this with two columns per entity: tax deferred, and tax attributed and unfunded.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's ledger is the heart of this lesson. On your personal balance sheet, a foreign company should be recorded at its value after the home tax that will be due when its profit comes home, not before it. Deferred tax is a liability you have chosen to pay later; it is still a liability. Attributed but unpaid tax is a current liability. And any unfiled reporting or unassessed tax for open years is a contingent liability that belongs in your liquidity planning until it is resolved. A balance sheet that counts the foreign company at its gross asset value overstates your wealth and understates your cash needs. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Family, legacy and what "enough" means

Deferral raises a question only you can answer. Money deferred for decades in a foreign company grows, but it is money you do not spend, and on your death it passes subject to whatever tax and estate rules then apply. So ask yourself: what is this deferred wealth for? Is it a business you are building, an inheritance you intend, or a number you are reluctant to stop growing?

There is no right answer, and no one should define it for you. But the answer changes the structure. Wealth meant to be spent should not be built to be hard to reach. Wealth meant for others needs an estate plan that knows where it is.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a foreign holding company's gross assets as personal wealth while its tax is deferred or attributed and unfunded. The control is a tax provision schedule beside your personal balance sheet, updated yearly, with cash set aside for every attributed amount.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner celebrates a low foreign tax rate as a permanent saving, when it is either a timing benefit with a measurable value, or, for passive income, nothing at all.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser on deferral and attribution, and accountant on the provision schedule.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick taught the personal balance sheet and the liquidity floor. Attributed income attacks the floor directly: it is a cash demand created by a company you control but cannot always draw from, so the floor must be sized with it in view.

Recap

Real deferral postpones home tax and is worth the present value of the postponement. Attribution removes deferral for passive income and creates a yearly cash call on the owner. Record both on your balance sheet: deferred tax as a liability, attributed tax as current, unresolved exposure as contingent.

Next: Vera on The Rules: reporting duties for foreign affiliates and property, and how Canada and Guyana approach them.
checklist: I can state the value of deferral for each active foreign company I own.
I know which foreign companies attribute income to me each year.
I keep a tax provision schedule beside my personal balance sheet.
I record foreign holdings at value after the home tax that will be due.
I have funded, or reserved for, every attributed tax amount.
I know whether dividends from already-attributed profits are taxed again.
I have asked myself what deferred wealth is for.
head: Field checklist
speak: Real deferral is an interest-free loan from my home government. If an active foreign company keeps its profit, the home tax I would owe on a dividend stays invested until the profit comes home. Its value is the present value of postponing that tax, which grows with the rate gap, the length of the deferral and the return on the retained money. In my hypothetical, postponing 150,000 dollars of tax for ten years was worth about 80,000 dollars today. Attribution reverses it. For passive income in a company I control, the home country taxes me each year on income I have not received, so I pay from my own cash while the company holds the money. Later dividends from those profits may not be taxed again, but my liquidity takes the hit. So on my balance sheet, deferred tax is a liability, attributed tax is current, and unresolved exposure is contingent.
terms: Value of deferral — the present value saved by paying a tax later rather than now.
Tax provision schedule — a record, per entity, of tax deferred, tax attributed and paid, and cash set aside.
Previously taxed income — profit already taxed in the shareholder's hands through attribution, often tracked so it is not taxed again when distributed.

hostile.q: Your personal statement values your foreign company at its full asset value. What tax sits behind that number?
hostile.a: I have restated it on the second page at value after home tax. The company's income is attributed to me each year, so the tax is paid annually and shown in my personal returns, with a reserve for the current year. There is no deferred tax on this one; there is a current cash call, and I have funded it separately from the project equity.

title: Reporting Duties: What Your Home Country Wants to See, Every Year
summary: Most countries require residents to report foreign companies, foreign property and foreign accounts on dedicated returns, separate from income tax. These duties often carry penalties for lateness or omission even when no tax is due, and they are increasingly checked against data that banks exchange automatically. Two Systems compares how Canada and Guyana approach the point, conceptually.
body:
The information return is a separate duty from tax, it often carries penalties even when no tax is owed, and your home authority may already see your foreign accounts through automatic bank reporting before you tell it anything.

Recall

Q. What does a distribution memo check?

A. That the corporate test, the lender's distribution conditions and the withholding obligation are each met, with evidence, before any payment to owners.

Q. What does a land-rich share clause in a treaty do?

A. It lets the country where real property sits tax gains on shares of a company whose value comes mainly from that property, so selling the company does not escape source tax.

Q. How is escalation different from contingency?

A. Escalation is the expected rise in prices over time and is estimated from the schedule and market indices. Contingency covers risks and unknowns. Mixing them hides both.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, records are where cross-border structures are judged in practice. An auditor or a bank rarely starts with the tax law; it starts by asking for the returns. If they exist, are on time and agree with each other, the conversation is about substance. If they are missing, the conversation is about penalties and credibility, and it may never get to substance. This lesson teaches concepts; every form, deadline, threshold and penalty must be verified against the primary source before you rely on it.

Three kinds of foreign reporting

In plain English: home authorities usually want to know three things about your life abroad. What companies you own or control. What property and investments you hold. And what accounts you keep.

The professional framing: these are often reported on separate information returns, each with its own threshold, below which no filing is needed, its own content, such as ownership percentages, financial statements, income types and transactions with you, and its own deadline, often tied to your income tax return [unverified — confirm independently]. Some cover individuals, some companies, some trusts and partnerships. A foreign affiliate return might ask for the affiliate's financial statements, its income by type, and every transaction between it and you. A foreign property return might ask for cost, income and gains on property above a value threshold.

A worked example, hypothetical. A developer owns 100 percent of a development company abroad, holds 30 percent of a second foreign company with partners, and keeps a foreign bank account with a balance well above most thresholds. That is potentially three or four returns a year: one per foreign affiliate, one for foreign property or accounts, and possibly one for any transfers to a foreign trust or partnership. Each must be filed even if the development company paid no dividends and owed no home tax.

Penalties that do not need a tax bill

Reporting penalties are often designed to bite on their own. Some systems charge a fixed amount per day late, up to a cap. Others charge a percentage of the value of the property or the cost of the investment for repeated or knowing failures [unverified — confirm independently]. And failing to report can extend the period in which an authority may reassess your income tax, so years you thought were closed may stay open.

Say that out loud now.

Tax and reporting are two duties; I can owe the second when I owe nothing on the first.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A developer misses three years of a foreign affiliate return. Under a hypothetical regime charging a fixed daily penalty with a cap per return, the penalty is the cap times three, before any question of tax. If the authority later finds the affiliate's income was attributable, the reassessment window for those years may also be extended because of the missing returns. A filing that would have taken a day a year has cost three caps and reopened three tax years.

Automatic exchange: your bank may report first

Many countries now participate in automatic exchange of financial account information, under which banks and other financial institutions identify account holders resident abroad and report their balances and income to the local authority, which passes them to the holder's home country [unverified — confirm independently]. The common framework is known as the Common Reporting Standard, and the United States has its own separate regime. The practical consequence is simple: assume your home authority knows about your foreign accounts. Your returns should match what it already sees.

Consistency across documents

One more records point. The same foreign company appears in many places: your information returns, your personal tax return, your bank's know-your-customer file, a lender's sponsor questionnaire, your personal financial statement, and possibly an investor's diligence. Each asks the ownership percentage, the value and the activity in slightly different words. Inconsistent answers, a 100 percent holding on one form and "minority interest" on another, or "operating business" to the bank and "investment holding" to the tax authority, are what auditors and credit officers look for first. Keep one master description of each entity and copy from it.

A practical habit: when any form asks about a foreign entity, keep a copy of the exact answer given, dated, in the register beside the entity. Then the next form can be checked against the last one in a minute.

Vera's records rule

Keep a foreign reporting register: each entity, property and account; the return it requires; the threshold test; the due date; who prepares it; the date filed; and where the filed copy and its working papers sit. Review it each year before your income tax return is prepared, and whenever you form, buy, sell or close anything abroad.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

Conceptually, and to be verified against the primary source in each country. Canada taxes residents on worldwide income and has detailed foreign affiliate rules, including attribution of foreign accrual property income, the Canadian name for passive income of controlled foreign affiliates. It requires information returns on foreign affiliates and on specified foreign property above a cost threshold, with significant penalties for late or missing filings, and participates in automatic exchange of financial account information [unverified — confirm independently]. Guyana's tax system has generally been described as having less developed rules specifically targeting controlled foreign companies, and its reporting regime for residents' foreign holdings is narrower; it has also made international transparency commitments [unverified — confirm independently]. The conceptual lesson: in a system like Canada's, the duty to report a foreign company can be as important as the tax on it; in a system with fewer specific rules, the absence of a rule is not permission, because general residence, anti-avoidance and record-keeping duties still apply. Verify every one of these points against current primary sources before relying on any of them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a missing information return discovered by a bank or an authority, which costs penalties, extends reassessment periods and damages credibility before substance is discussed. The control is a foreign reporting register reviewed every year and on every transaction abroad.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that if no tax is owed, no return is needed, or that a foreign account he never told anyone about is invisible. Neither is safe.

Professional sign-off required: home-country tax adviser on which returns apply, and accountant on their preparation.

Callback

In Week 56, Elias and Ford taught the substance record: evidence made at the time, kept where the decisions are made. The foreign reporting register is the same discipline turned toward your home authority: one list, one owner, filed copies you can produce in an hour, built as you go rather than reconstructed when someone asks.

Recap

Foreign companies, property and accounts are usually reported on separate information returns, with their own thresholds, contents and deadlines. Penalties can arise without any tax, and missing returns can keep tax years open. Automatic exchange means your bank may report first. Keep a register and review it every year.

Next: Nadia on The Numbers: attributing passive income step by step, with relief for foreign tax.
checklist: I keep a foreign reporting register for every entity, property and account.
I know the threshold test for each information return.
I know each return's due date and who prepares it.
I file every return even when no tax is owed.
I keep filed copies and working papers where I can produce them in an hour.
My returns agree with what banks report under automatic exchange.
I review the register yearly and on every transaction abroad.
head: Field checklist
speak: Reporting is a separate duty from tax. Most countries want residents to report three things on information returns: foreign companies they own or control, foreign property and investments above a threshold, and foreign accounts. Each return has its own threshold, content and deadline, and many must be filed even when no tax is owed. Penalties often bite on their own, as daily amounts with caps or as percentages of value for knowing failures, and a missing return can keep tax years open longer. Banks in many countries now report foreign account holders automatically to their home authorities, so I assume my home authority already knows. Canada has detailed foreign affiliate rules and information returns with serious penalties; Guyana's specific rules are narrower, but the absence of a rule is not permission. My control is a foreign reporting register, reviewed every year and on every transaction abroad.
terms: Information return — a filing reporting foreign holdings or transactions, separate from the income tax return.
Automatic exchange of information — the routine reporting of foreign account holders' balances and income by financial institutions, passed between tax authorities.
Foreign reporting register — a list of every foreign entity, property and account, with the return each requires, its due date and its status.

hostile.q: Our records show foreign account balances in your name. Were they reported?
hostile.a: Yes. Every account is on my foreign reporting register, with the return it falls under, the filing date and the filed copy. The balances and income on those returns agree with the bank statements, and I can provide both. If any figure differs from what you hold, I would like to see it so we can reconcile it today.

title: Attributing Passive Income, Step by Step
summary: Work a hypothetical controlled foreign company with mixed income through attribution: separate active from passive, compute the passive amount, apply relief for foreign tax, and find the home tax due this year. Then track what happens when the company pays a dividend later. All rates and thresholds are hypothetical.
body:
Attribution is arithmetic you can do on one page: split the income, measure the passive part, give relief for foreign tax, and tax the rest at home this year, then make sure you are not taxed on it again when it comes home.

Recall

Q. What three questions does every controlled-foreign-company regime ask?

A. Is the company controlled by home residents? Is the income active or passive? And how much foreign tax has it already paid?

Q. Why is foreign tax above the credit cap wasted?

A. Because most credit systems will not credit more than their own tax on that income, so excess foreign tax gives no relief unless domestic law allows a carryover.

Q. In earned value, what does the cost performance index measure?

A. Earned value divided by actual cost: how much work was achieved for each dollar spent. Below 1.0 means overrunning.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, attribution rules are complex in law but simple in shape. If you can do this page yourself, you can check your adviser's number, see which income is driving the tax, and decide whether to restructure. Every rate, threshold and relief mechanism below is hypothetical and chosen only to show the arithmetic; verify the real ones against the primary source before you rely on them.

The setup

A developer resident in Country R owns 100 percent of a company in Country F. Country F taxes companies at a hypothetical 10 percent. Country R taxes individuals at a hypothetical 30 percent on attributed income and gives relief for foreign tax by a credit. This year the F company earns:

IncomeAmount, dollarsCharacter
Profit from developing and selling units, own staff of ten1,500,000Active
Net rent from a building managed by an outside agent400,000Passive
Interest on surplus cash deposits100,000Passive

Step 1: classify and total

Active income: 1,500,000 dollars. Passive income: 400,000 plus 100,000, which is 500,000 dollars. Total profit: 2,000,000 dollars. Only the passive 500,000 dollars is a candidate for attribution.

Step 2: foreign tax on the passive part

F taxes all profit at 10 percent, 200,000 dollars in total. The share on the passive income is 10 percent of 500,000 dollars, 50,000 dollars. Allocate foreign tax to the income it relates to; do not credit tax on active income against attributed passive income.

Step 3: home tax before relief

Attributed amount: 500,000 dollars. Home tax at 30 percent: 150,000 dollars.

Step 4: relief for foreign tax

Credit for the 50,000 dollars of foreign tax on the passive income, within the cap of 150,000 dollars. Home tax payable this year: 100,000 dollars.

Say that out loud now.

Classify, total the passive, allocate the foreign tax to it, tax at home, credit within the cap.

Some regimes give relief differently, for example by deducting from the attributed amount a figure that grosses up the foreign tax, rather than a direct credit [unverified — confirm independently]. Run this version too. If relief were a deduction of foreign tax grossed up by the home rate, 50,000 divided by 0.30 is about 166,667 dollars, so the attributed amount falls to 333,333 dollars, and home tax at 30 percent is 100,000 dollars. In this simple case the two methods agree; with different rates and caps they need not.

Step 5: track it for later

The developer has now been taxed on 500,000 dollars he has not received. Record it in a schedule of previously taxed income: the year, the amount attributed and the tax paid. When the F company later pays a dividend, many systems let the part paid out of previously taxed income come home without further tax, or with a deduction [unverified — confirm independently]. Without the schedule, the developer may be taxed twice on the same rent.

A second worked example: moving the line

Suppose the developer hires a property team in F and the rental business meets the home country's active-business test. The 400,000 dollars of rent becomes active. Passive income falls to the 100,000 dollars of interest. Foreign tax on it: 10,000 dollars. Home tax: 30,000 dollars, less the 10,000 dollar credit, 20,000 dollars this year. Attributed tax falls from 100,000 to 20,000 dollars.

But price the change honestly. If the property team costs a hypothetical 250,000 dollars a year, and the 80,000 dollars of home tax saved is only deferred, not removed, because the rent will be taxed when it comes home, then the trade is 250,000 dollars a year of real cost for the timing value of deferring 80,000 dollars. At an 8 percent cost of capital, deferring 80,000 dollars for five years is worth about 25,600 dollars. The team does not pay for itself on tax grounds. It might on operating grounds, if it manages the building better, and that is the only honest reason to hire it.

A third worked example: the dividend that follows

Three years later, the F company pays the developer a dividend of 1,200,000 dollars. The schedule of previously taxed income shows 500,000 dollars attributed in each of the three years, 1,500,000 dollars in total, all still undistributed. Under a regime that treats distributions as coming first out of previously taxed income, the whole 1,200,000 dollars is paid out of it, and no further home tax arises on the dividend itself, though F may withhold on it and the relief for that withholding needs its own check [unverified — confirm independently]. The schedule then shows 300,000 dollars of previously taxed income remaining.

Without the schedule, the developer's return might have treated the 1,200,000 dollars as an ordinary foreign dividend and taxed it again, about 360,000 dollars at the hypothetical 30 percent rate, on money already taxed. That is why Nadia keeps the schedule beside the worksheet and updates both every year: the attribution saves nothing if the record of it is lost.

What the page tells you

Before reading the lessons, check the page itself. Every number on it should trace to a source document: the income split to the foreign company's accounts, the foreign tax to its tax computation, the rate to the current home rules, and the previously taxed balance to last year's worksheet. A worksheet you cannot trace is a worksheet an auditor will rebuild, and their version will not be kinder than yours.

Two things. First, the interest on surplus cash is small but always passive: a company sitting on idle cash abroad generates attributed income for no business reason, so sweep it or put it to work. Second, the substance needed to turn passive into active costs real money, and the saving is usually timing. Decide on business grounds, then let tax follow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is applying foreign tax on active income as a credit against attributed passive income, or forgetting the previously taxed income schedule, so the home tax is wrong in both directions. The control is a one-page attribution worksheet for each controlled foreign company, each year, with the allocation of foreign tax shown.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hires staff abroad to make income active, purely for tax, without pricing the staff against the timing value of the deferral. It is often a loss dressed as a saving.

Professional sign-off required: home-country tax adviser on classification and relief, and accountant on the worksheet and the previously taxed income schedule.

Callback

In Week 57, Elias worked one income stream through credit and exemption, with the credit cap. Attribution uses the same cap and the same allocation discipline. The new step is that the income is taxed before it moves, which is why the previously taxed income schedule exists.

Recap

Classify the income, total the passive part, allocate foreign tax to it, tax it at home, and credit within the cap. Record what was attributed so later dividends are not taxed twice. Turning passive into active costs real money and usually buys only deferral.

Next: Cole on The Room: the tax authority's interview about a foreign affiliate.
checklist: I have an attribution worksheet for each controlled foreign company each year.
I classify every income stream as active or passive, with reasons.
I allocate foreign tax to the income it relates to.
I credit foreign tax only within the cap.
I keep a schedule of previously taxed income by year.
I sweep idle cash out of foreign companies or put it to work.
I price any substance added to make income active against the deferral it buys.
head: Field checklist
speak: Attribution fits on one page. First, I classify the foreign company's income: development profit earned by its own staff is active; rent collected by an outside agent and interest on deposits are passive. Second, I total the passive part, 500,000 dollars in my hypothetical. Third, I allocate the foreign tax that relates to it, here 50,000 dollars, and never use tax on active income. Fourth, I tax the passive amount at home, 150,000 dollars, and credit the foreign tax within the cap, leaving 100,000 dollars due this year. Fifth, I record the 500,000 dollars as previously taxed income, so a later dividend from it is not taxed again. If I hire a property team to make the rent active, attributed tax falls, but the saving is mostly deferral, and in my example the team cost far more than the deferral was worth. Decide on business grounds, then let tax follow.
terms: Attribution worksheet — a yearly calculation classifying a foreign company's income and computing the home tax on its attributed part.
Allocation of foreign tax — matching foreign tax to the specific income it was charged on, before using it as relief.
Active-business test — the conditions under which income, such as rent, is treated as earned by an active business rather than as passive.

hostile.q: You credited 50,000 dollars of foreign tax against the attributed income. How did you get that number?
hostile.a: From the foreign company's tax computation. It paid 200,000 dollars on 2,000,000 dollars of profit. I allocated the tax to each income stream at the same 10 percent rate, so 50,000 dollars relates to the 500,000 dollars of passive income. I did not use the tax on the active development profit. The worksheet shows the allocation line by line, and our adviser has confirmed the method.

title: The Tax Authority's Interview About Your Foreign Affiliate
summary: A tax auditor is asking how a foreign company you control earns its income and why none of it was attributed. The scene shows how to prepare, what to bring, the lines to say and never to say, the question behind the auditor's questions, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state. Your adviser leads on law; you answer on facts.
body:
In a tax interview about a foreign affiliate, your job is to answer questions of fact accurately and briefly, let your adviser handle questions of law, and never guess, because the auditor is building a record and every sentence you say goes into it.

Recall

Q. In the composite case of the offshore rental company, what was the point of no return?

A. The bank's due-diligence question in year 7, after which a voluntary disclosure was likely no longer available and the choices narrowed to paying and explaining.

Q. In tax diligence, what should you offer when a buyer finds an exposure?

A. A sized figure for the open years, including interest and penalty, and a specific mechanism to allocate it, such as a capped indemnity or an escrow released as years close.

Q. What is cost to complete?

A. A forecast of what it will actually take to finish the project from today, given what is now known, as distinct from budget remaining.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you own companies abroad, a home-country audit of them is a matter of when, not if. The outcome depends mostly on two things: whether your records support your position, and how you behave in the room. Records you build in advance. Behaviour you prepare. This lesson is about the second, and assumes the first.

The scene

A meeting room at the tax authority, or a video call. Across the table: an auditor and a senior reviewer. Your side: you and your tax adviser. The subject, hypothetically, is a company in a low-tax country that you control, which earned 600,000 dollars last year from managing and leasing a building, none of which you attributed to yourself, because your adviser classified the rental business as active.

The auditor opens: "Tell us how the company earns its income. Who does the work?"

Before the meeting

Prepare with your adviser for at least one session. Agree who answers what: you answer facts about the business, your adviser answers questions about the law and the classification. Read your own information returns and the attribution worksheet again, so you do not contradict them. Assemble the evidence the classification depends on: the employment contracts of the company's property staff, payroll records, the management agreement if any, the leases, the maintenance contracts, the board minutes deciding on leasing and capital works. Check your adviser's engagement covers the audit; Week 25 taught you why that matters.

The lines to say

Answer the question asked, with facts, in plain sentences. "The company employs four full-time people in the country: a property manager, a leasing officer, a maintenance supervisor and an accountant. They find tenants, negotiate leases, manage repairs and keep the books. Here are their contracts and last year's payroll." Then stop.

If you do not know: "I don't know that figure. I'll confirm it in writing by Friday." Write it down in front of them, and deliver it.

If the question is about the law: "That's a question on the classification. My adviser will answer it."

Say that out loud now.

I answer facts, my adviser answers law, and I never guess.

The lines never to say

Never speculate about what an employee "probably" does; ask the auditor whether you may confirm it. Never say "it's just a holding company" as a figure of speech; the words will be quoted against an active-business classification. Never volunteer opinions on what the rules should be. Never say "my accountant handled all that"; it sounds like distance from your own company, and the auditor will ask why you do not know. And never change a fact between meetings. If you later find you were wrong, correct it in writing, promptly.

The question behind the question

"Who does the work?" is really "is this an active business or a passive investment with a label?" Every follow-up tests the same thing. Who decides on new leases? Where are they decided? Who signs the repair contracts? Are the staff really employed by this company, or by a related service firm that bills it? Is the staff's time spent on this building or spread across others? Each fact moves the classification one way or the other.

A worked example, hypothetical. The auditor finds that three of the four staff are employed by a management company that also serves eleven other owners, and bills your company 120,000 dollars a year. That fact may weaken an active-business classification that depended on the company's own employees. If attribution follows, 600,000 dollars of income is attributed at a hypothetical 30 percent home rate, 180,000 dollars, less any foreign tax credit. Your adviser's answer is legal: whether outsourced staff count under the rules. Your answer is factual: the contract, the hours, the decisions the company's own officer makes.

A second worked example. The reviewer asks for minutes showing who approved last year's largest lease, a ten-year lease worth 300,000 dollars a year. You produce minutes signed in the foreign country by the company's resident director, with the leasing officer's recommendation attached. That one document does more than an hour of explanation, because it shows a decision made by the company's own people, where the company is.

After the interview

Within two days, your adviser should send the auditor a short written note: the documents provided, the points you undertook to confirm and the date each will arrive. Meet every date. Keep your own note of what was asked and answered, made the same day, while it is fresh; an audit may run for months and memories diverge. If the auditor issues a proposal to reassess, read it with your adviser for factual errors first, because a wrong fact in a proposal is far easier to correct than a wrong conclusion drawn from it.

And keep the business running exactly as it did. Changing how the foreign company operates in the middle of an audit, hiring staff suddenly or moving decisions, will be read as an admission that the old way did not meet the test. If a change is genuinely needed, make it on business grounds, document why, and let your adviser decide when to tell the auditor.

When to stay silent

After every answer, stop. The auditor's silence is not a request for more. Most damaging statements in audits are the second and third sentences of an answer the first sentence had already finished. And if your adviser asks for a short break, take it, even mid-question.

Holding your state

An auditor is not your enemy; they are doing a job with a file and a deadline. Be courteous, be on time, and bring copies. If you feel defensive, slow your breathing while you listen, and answer a fraction more slowly than feels natural. Short, accurate, calm answers are the most persuasive thing you can bring.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who talks too much, speculates about facts, or describes his own company in words that contradict its filings. The control is preparation with your adviser, a clear division of who answers what, and the discipline of "I'll confirm by Friday."

The beginner's mistake

The beginner arrives without the evidence the classification relies on, expecting to explain it. In an audit, explanation is cheap and documents are evidence.

Professional sign-off required: tax adviser or tax lawyer present at the interview, engaged for the audit.

Callback

Four lessons back, Ford and Cole showed a developer who never filed. This room is what filing buys you: an auditor asking whether your classification is right, rather than why your returns do not exist. The first conversation is about facts. The second is about penalties.

Recap

Prepare with your adviser, bring the evidence, answer facts briefly and accurately, pass questions of law to your adviser, never guess, and confirm anything you do not know in writing. The question behind every question is whether the business is real.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on foreign affiliates, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill.
checklist: My adviser's engagement letter covers the audit.
I have prepared with my adviser and agreed who answers what.
I have reread my information returns and attribution worksheet.
I have the evidence the classification relies on, in copies.
I answer facts briefly and pass questions of law to my adviser.
I write down every point to confirm, and confirm it in writing on time.
I correct any mistaken statement promptly, in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: When an auditor asks about a foreign company I control, I prepare with my adviser first and agree who answers what. I answer facts about the business, and my adviser answers questions of law and classification. I reread my own returns and worksheet so I do not contradict them, and I bring the evidence: staff contracts, payroll, leases, minutes. In the room I answer the question asked, briefly, and stop. If I do not know, I say I will confirm it in writing by Friday, and I do. I never speculate, never call it just a holding company, and never say my accountant handled everything. The question behind every question is whether the business is real or a label, so a single set of minutes showing a decision made by the company's own people, where the company is, is worth an hour of explanation. Short, accurate, calm answers persuade.
terms: Audit interview — a meeting in which a tax authority asks a taxpayer and adviser questions of fact and law about a filed position.
Division of answers — the agreed split between owner and adviser on who answers factual and who answers legal questions.
Evidence of activity — documents, such as employment contracts, payroll, leases and minutes, showing that a business is actively run by its own people.

hostile.q: Three of your four staff are employed by a management firm that serves other owners. How is this an active business rather than an outsourced investment?
hostile.a: On the facts, my adviser will address how the rules treat outsourced staff. What I can tell you is what the company itself does: its resident officer decides every lease and capital commitment, as these minutes show; the management firm works under a contract specifying dedicated hours for this building; and the company bears the leasing and repair risk itself. I'll send the time records for the dedicated staff by Friday.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 59 Review: Foreign Affiliates, Attribution and Reporting
summary: Six questions test the week: deferral, the three CFC questions, rent as passive income, reporting as a separate duty, the value of deferral, and attribution arithmetic. A Red Pen drill finds the defects in a hypothetical structure note, and a boardroom drill asks you to explain foreign affiliates in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: a foreign company defers home tax only when it runs a real active business, passive income in a company you control is usually taxed at home every year, and the reporting is owed either way.

Recall

Q. On a personal balance sheet, how should deferred and attributed foreign tax be recorded?

A. Deferred tax as a liability you have chosen to pay later, attributed but unpaid tax as a current liability, and unresolved exposure for open years as a contingent liability.

Q. What is a principal purpose test?

A. A treaty clause denying a benefit where obtaining it was one of the principal purposes of the arrangement, unless granting it fits the treaty's object and purpose.

Q. What is the difference between a bid package and a trade?

A. A trade is a type of work, such as concrete or electrical. A bid package is a defined scope offered for pricing, which may combine trades or split one, organised to get competitive and complete bids.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you own anything abroad through a company, these questions apply to you every year. If you can answer them without notes, you can tell when a structure's deferral is real and when it is an assumption. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is deferral, and why do governments limit it?

Answer: Deferral is postponing home tax on a foreign company's profit until it is paid out. Governments limit it because easily movable passive income could otherwise sit in low-tax companies indefinitely.

Question 2. What three questions does a controlled-foreign-company regime ask?

Answer: Whether home residents control the foreign company, whether its income is active or passive, and how much foreign tax it has already paid.

Question 3. Why is rent the tricky income type?

Answer: Because rental income is often treated as passive unless the company runs an active rental business at the scale the rules require, such as with enough of its own staff managing the property. The line depends on what the company actually does.

Question 4. Can you owe a penalty for a foreign information return when no tax is due?

Answer: Yes. Reporting is a separate duty, often with fixed or value-based penalties, and missing returns can also keep tax years open longer.

Question 5. How is real deferral valued?

Answer: As the present value saved by paying the home tax later rather than now, which grows with the rate gap, the length of deferral and the return on the retained money. It is a timing benefit, not a rate cut.

Question 6. A controlled foreign company has 500,000 dollars of passive income, foreign tax of 50,000 dollars on it, and a home rate of 30 percent with a credit. What home tax is due this year?

Answer: 30 percent of 500,000 dollars is 150,000 dollars, less the 50,000 dollar credit, so 100,000 dollars, and the 500,000 dollars is recorded as previously taxed income.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Elias drew the line between active income that earns deferral and passive income that is attributed. Ford and Cole took a composite case of an offshore rental company that never filed, giving Rule 59. Warrick valued deferral and placed attributed tax on the personal balance sheet. Vera taught reporting duties and automatic exchange, and compared Canada and Guyana. Nadia worked an attribution step by step. Cole ran the tax authority's interview.

The Red Pen

Find the defects in this hypothetical structure note before reading on.

Structure Note: Offshore Holdco. Holdco, incorporated in a zero-tax country, will own the three rental buildings, transferred from the founder at cost. Rent will be collected by the local agent. Because Holdco will not pay dividends for ten years, no home tax arises until then, giving full deferral. Surplus cash will be held on deposit by Holdco. No home filings are needed while no dividends are paid. The incorporation agent has confirmed the structure is compliant. Prepared by the founder.

The defects. First, rent collected by an agent, in a company with no staff, is likely passive income, so attribution may apply every year and there may be no deferral at all. Second, interest on surplus cash deposits is passive income too, adding to attribution. Third, "no home filings are needed" confuses tax with reporting; information returns on the foreign company are likely due every year. Fourth, transferring the buildings "at cost" ignores that a transfer to a company you own may be a taxable disposition at value. Fifth, the incorporation agent is not engaged to advise on the founder's home tax, so its confirmation covers only its own country. Sixth, there is no home-country adviser sign-off and no classification of the income. Seventh, a zero-tax country means no foreign tax to credit, so any attributed income is taxed at the full home rate.

Now write the corrected note in three lines: Holdco's rent and interest are expected to be passive and attributed annually, and are modelled at the home rate; information returns are filed each year, on the register; and the transfer of the buildings is reviewed by a home-country adviser for tax at value before it happens. Notice that the corrected note promises less and is worth more.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks, "Why don't we just put the rental buildings in an offshore company and pay no tax until we take the money out?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because for rental income that usually doesn't work. A foreign company we control defers home tax only on active business income, earned by real people running a real business there. Passive income, such as rent collected by an agent, interest and portfolio gains, is usually caught by our country's controlled-foreign-company rules and taxed in our hands every year, as if paid to us, whether or not anything moves. A zero-tax country makes it worse, because there is no foreign tax to credit. On top of that, we would owe yearly information returns on the company, with penalties even if no tax were due, and moving the buildings into it could itself be taxed. If the company ran a genuine active rental business with its own staff, some deferral might survive, but the staff cost usually exceeds the value of postponing the tax. So the right question is whether the structure makes business sense first. If it does, we classify the income each year with a home adviser, file every return, and plan the cash for any attributed tax."

Score yourself. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the three questions? Did you separate tax from reporting? Did you finish inside two minutes?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is believing that foreign means deferred. The control: an annual classification of every foreign entity by a home-country adviser, and a reporting register, before the tax year closes.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking a low foreign tax rate is always a saving. For passive income in a controlled company, it usually means full home tax, now.

Callback

In Week 55, Omar taught structure as design, with six lenses and the flow of funds. This week added a seventh question to the tax lens for every foreign box on the chart: is its income active or passive, and what does home law do with it each year?

Recap

Deferral survives for real active business abroad. Controlled-foreign-company rules attribute passive income to home owners yearly, with relief for foreign tax. Reporting is a separate duty with its own penalties. Value deferral as timing, record attributed tax honestly, and keep a register. Rule 59 puts a home-country adviser on every foreign entity before the first transfer.

Next: Omar, with Nadia, on First Principles: financing the structure, debt versus equity, thin capitalisation and documented intercompany loans.
checklist: What is deferral, and why do governments limit it?
What three questions does a controlled-foreign-company regime ask?
Why is rent the tricky income type?
Can you owe a penalty for a foreign information return when no tax is due?
How is real deferral valued?
A controlled foreign company has 500,000 dollars of passive income, foreign tax of 50,000 dollars on it, and a home rate of 30 percent with a credit. What home tax is due this year?
head: The six questions
speak: Foreign affiliates came down to one sentence this week: a foreign company defers home tax only when it runs a real active business, passive income in a company I control is usually taxed at home every year, and the reporting is owed either way. Controlled-foreign-company regimes ask three questions: control, the character of the income, and the foreign tax paid. Rent is the tricky case: often passive unless the company runs an active rental business with its own people. Attribution gives relief for foreign tax within a cap, and I track previously taxed income so later dividends are not taxed twice. Real deferral is a timing benefit worth the present value of postponing tax, not a rate cut, and adding staff abroad purely to earn it rarely pays. Reporting is separate, with penalties even when no tax is owed. Rule 59: never form, fund or keep a foreign company without a home-country adviser classifying it and naming its reports.
terms: Foreign affiliate — a foreign company in which a resident holds a significant interest, as defined by home-country rules.
Previously taxed income schedule — a record of income already attributed and taxed, used to avoid taxing it again when distributed.
Classification review — the yearly assessment, by a home-country adviser, of whether each foreign entity's income is active or passive.

hostile.q: You say the foreign company defers tax. Show me why its income isn't attributed to you every year.
hostile.a: I'll show you the classification, not just assert it. Here is my home adviser's yearly review: the company develops and sells units with its own staff of ten, so that profit is active and not attributed. Its interest on surplus cash is passive, and I attribute it and pay the home tax each year, as the worksheet shows. Every information return is filed and on the register. If the activity changes, the review is redone.
